# AN/PRC-117G Radio
The AN/PRC-117G is the standard manpack radio for radio operators. It can hold up to four nets, reaches much farther than a headset, extends friendly radio coverage to everyone around you, doubles as a field phone, and even has a small storage compartment.
Just been handed one? Start with [bold]Your first five minutes[/bold]. That is enough to get you on the air. The rest of this guide explains what the set can do once you are comfortable with the basics.
The radio has two control interfaces:
- [textlink="Guided panel, control by control" link="AU14CommsANPRCGuided"] - the standard interface. It handles the essentials for you and keeps the radio in AUTO. - [textlink="Expert faceplate, key by key" link="AU14CommsANPRCExpert"] - the radio's own keypad and display. It can do everything the guided panel can, plus several advanced operator functions.
## Your first five minutes
You do not need to understand the entire radio before using it. Do this:
1. [bold]Wear the pack[/bold] in your back slot. If it is in your hands or lying on the ground, it is not providing relay coverage. 2. [bold]Open the radio panel.[/bold] Alt-click the pack, or right-click it, and choose [bold]Open Radio Panel[/bold]. The first time you do this, a short briefing appears; press [bold]GOT IT[/bold]. 3. On the NETS tab, press [bold]LOAD STANDARD NETS[/bold]. This switches the radio on, loads your squad and command nets, and selects your squad net for transmission. 4. [bold]Load your fill card.[/bold] You should have one in your pocket. Use it on the pack. The SECURITY tab should now show [bold]ENCRYPTED[/bold]. 5. [bold]Talk.[/bold] Type [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] followed by your message. You transmit on whichever memory is marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold], using your callsign. 6. [bold]Keep an eye on the banner[/bold] below the radio display. If something needs attention, it tells you what is wrong and usually gives you a button to fix it. Green means the set is ready.
That is enough to get started.
One last thing: [bold]carry a spare power cell.[/bold] See [bold]Battery[/bold] below.
## Who can use the radio
Some functions require radio-operator training.
A trained operator can open the control panel, transmit directly through the pack with [color=#a4885c]:r[/color], and provide relay coverage while wearing it.
The handset and field phone do [bold]not[/bold] require training. Anyone can use them.
### GOVFOR and OPFOR trained roles
- Commander, Adjutant, and staff officers - Engineering and intelligence officers - Synthetics - Squad Leaders and Fireteam Leaders - Radio Traffic Operators
### CLF trained roles
- Cell Leader - Radio Operator
Anyone can permanently learn to operate the set by reading a [bold]field radio operator's pamphlet[/bold].
Ordinary headset users do not need radio training. They only need to be within relay range of a powered radio carrying their net.
## You are the relay
Combat radio nets are [bold]relay-gated[/bold]. A headset only works while it is within range of something carrying that net.
A powered AN/PRC worn by a trained operator acts as that relay. It anchors [bold]every friendly combat net loaded into its memory[/bold], not just the one currently marked ON AIR.
In other words: if your squad's net is loaded, nearby squad headsets work. If it is not loaded, they do not.
Your relay range depends on the antenna fitted to the radio:
[bold]Antenna[/bold] [bold]Clear[/bold] [bold]Degraded[/bold] [bold]Notes[/bold]
WHIP 30 tiles 45 tiles Standard antenna. Works normally while moving.
WIRE 35 tiles 50 tiles Range is halved while moving.
MAST 55 tiles 80 tiles Range is halved while moving. Best suited to command posts and staked radios.
Output power modifies those ranges:
- [bold]LO[/bold] - 60% - [bold]MED[/bold] - 100% - [bold]HI[/bold] - 150%
Relay coverage also reaches one level above and below the radio.
Output power is changed from the expert faceplate. The guided panel keeps the set on MED.
## Nets and memories
The AN/PRC has up to [bold]four memory slots[/bold]. Each slot can contain either a named radio net, such as your squad or command net, or a direct frequency.
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] always transmits on the memory marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold]. Press [bold]USE[/bold] beside another memory to make that one active.
- [bold]LOAD STANDARD NETS[/bold] fills empty memories with your standard squad and command nets. It will not overwrite anything you tuned manually. - [bold]EDIT[/bold] lets you select a net, rename the memory, or clear it. Your squad net and other standard nets appear near the top of the list. - If your search receiver identifies an enemy net, it appears with an [bold][INTERCEPT][/bold] tag. You may listen to and log it, but your radio will never relay it. - [bold]Direct frequencies[/bold] are entered from the expert faceplate. They are unrelayed, unencrypted, and effectively point-to-point radio channels. Entering a frequency that belongs to one of your known nets simply loads that net instead.
## Handset
Anyone can use the handset, even without radio-operator training.
Alt-click the [bold]person wearing the radio[/bold], or a radio that has been staked down, and select [bold]Take Handset[/bold].
- Anything you say normally while holding the handset is transmitted over the radio's ON AIR net using [bold]your own[/bold] callsign. - Whispering does not transmit. - The cord reaches roughly two and a half tiles. Go farther and the handset snaps back to the set. - Only one person can use it at a time. - Use the handset in your hand with Z, or select [bold]Hang Up Handset[/bold], to return it.
This lets someone such as a squad leader use an attached radio operator's set to speak on command even when their own headset cannot access that net.
## Phone
The AN/PRC can also act as a field telephone.
It can call other AN/PRC sets as well as fixed telephones at command posts and aboard ships. Those stations can call you in return.
- To place a call, use the [bold]AN/PRC-117G phone[/bold] action, choose [bold]Use Phone[/bold] on the set, or press [bold]PHONE[/bold] on the panel. Then select a station from the phone book. - When the radio rings, the wearer is told who is calling. [bold]Taking the handset answers the call.[/bold] The phone action can also be used to answer. - If somebody is already holding the handset when a call arrives, they join the call immediately. - While a call is connected, the handset belongs to the phone link. Anything spoken through it goes to the other station instead of the radio net. - [bold]Returning the handset hangs up.[/bold]
The phone book identifies stations by [bold]callsign[/bold], not by character name.
A radio also belongs to whichever side supplied its [bold]fill card[/bold], not necessarily the person carrying it. A set without a card cannot place or receive calls. A captured radio that still contains your side's fill card can therefore call your stations.
Phone calls still use radio.
Both stations must be switched on, worn or staked, charged, outside heavy jamming, and not in EMCON. They must also either be within roughly 45 tiles of each other, or both be connected to relay coverage through their side's command net.
If you cannot reach a station, it will not appear in the phone book. If the radio link disappears during a call, the call drops.
Every spoken line also consumes power and may expose the transmission to direction finding.
## Bag
The AN/PRC has the same storage compartment as the old AN/PRC-55 radio pack: a five-by-two inventory that accepts items up to Large size.
Click the pack to open it.
Fill cards, antennas, and power cells use their dedicated slots before entering the bag.
Be aware that the storage compartment of a [bold]staked radio is accessible to anyone standing beside it[/bold].
## Battery
The radio runs from a power cell, and active radio work drains one surprisingly quickly.
[bold]Carry spares.[/bold]
The radio operator's equipment rack provides three high-capacity cells, while an AN/PRC resupply crate contains another two.
[bold]What the set is doing[/bold] [bold]High-capacity cell lasts about[/bold]
Switched on, not relaying 80 minutes
Relaying for your squad 55 minutes
Normal radio-operator use: relaying and transmitting 40 to 45 minutes
Searching the band Much faster - search adds 3 per second
Transmitting costs additional power. So do radio checks, phone traffic, and retransmissions. Frequency hopping and HI output increase the cost further.
The expert faceplate provides [bold]POWER SAVE[/bold] and [bold]EMCON[/bold] modes when endurance matters. Its [bold]ENDURANCE[/bold] display estimates how many minutes remain at the radio's current drain.
Once the cell is empty, the set switches itself off. Replace the cell in the radio's dedicated cell slot, then switch the set back on.
## Callsigns
Radio traffic identifies people by [bold]callsign[/bold].
Your character's name and job title are not transmitted through headsets or the AN/PRC. Friendly and enemy listeners hear your callsign instead. Ordinary face-to-face speech is unaffected.
Callsigns are assigned automatically at deployment.
[bold]Example[/bold] [bold]Station[/bold]
HAVOC 6 Commanding officer
HAVOC 5 Executive officer or second-in-command
HAVOC 7 Senior non-commissioned officer
HAVOC ROMEO Command radio operator
HAVOC OPS Staff officers
SABRE ACTUAL Sabre (Alpha) squad leader
SABRE ROMEO Radio operator attached to Sabre (Alpha)
SABRE 1-1 ... 1-N Sabre (Alpha) squad members
[bold]ACTUAL[/bold] means the person in command is speaking personally, rather than somebody transmitting on their behalf.
A worn radio normally uses the [bold]wearer's callsign[/bold]. The faceplate shows this as AUTO, and the callsign follows the wearer through squad changes and equipment handovers.
Command posts and other staked stations can instead be assigned a fixed [bold]station callsign[/bold] from the faceplate's OPT page.
The [bold]Comms Net Directory[/bold], available through NET DIRECTORY on the panel as well as command-post laptops and overwatch consoles, shows which station currently holds each callsign.
For standard radio wording and prowords, see [textlink="Voice Procedure" link="AU14CommsVoiceProcedure"].
## Encryption (COMSEC)
Your faction's radio encryption is stored on a physical [bold]COMSEC fill card[/bold].
With a current card loaded, secured traffic from your radio is heard as static by enemy interceptors who lack the matching key.
- [bold]No card[/bold] - the radio still works, but your transmissions go out in the clear. The set warns you when this happens. - [bold]PT mode[/bold] - deliberately sends traffic in the clear even if a valid fill card is installed. - [bold]ZEROIZE[/bold] - ejects the fill card into your hand. - [bold]DESTROY[/bold] - destroys the installed card. If the radio is about to be captured, either ZEROIZE or DESTROY it. - [bold]RECRYPTO[/bold] - available only with command authority. It replaces your faction's current encryption key, immediately superseding every existing card, including captured ones. Replacement cards must then come through supply unless an expert operator distributes the new key over the air from the faceplate's SEC page. - A current [bold]captured enemy fill card[/bold] allows your radio to read that faction's secured traffic until they perform a recrypto.
## Waveforms
The radio supports several transmission modes, each with different trade-offs.
[bold]Mode[/bold] [bold]Good for[/bold] [bold]Costs[/bold]
[bold]FH[/bold] frequency hop (AUTO) Reduces jamming by one tier. 1.5x battery cost per transmission and a small direction-finding signature.
[bold]SC[/bold] single channel Low power cost. Secured SC produces no DF signature. No resistance to jamming.
[bold]CT[/bold] cipher text Hidden and unreadable without the matching fill card. No DF signature. Requires a fill card. Ordinary headsets cannot receive it.
[bold]PT[/bold] plain text Uses half the normal battery cost. Anyone can read it, and it creates the largest DF risk.
Waveforms are selected from the expert faceplate.
The guided panel leaves the radio in FH.
## Jamming and direction finding
Jamming interferes with radio traffic rather than simply shutting it off.
A manpack can still transmit inside a jammer field, but the message may arrive degraded. FH reduces jamming by one tier. Heavy jamming also disables field-phone links.
Enemy electronic-warfare equipment may be able to locate the point from which you transmitted.
Things that increase your direction-finding risk include:
- PT transmissions - faction-net traffic sent without a fill card - FH transmissions - HI output power - repeated transmissions from the same position - transmitting near a jammer
Secured SC and CT transmissions produce no DF signature.
The expert faceplate's [bold]BURST[/bold] function halves your detection chance. [bold]EMCON[/bold] removes it entirely.
The [bold]RADIO CHECK[/bold] button transmits [bold]RADIO CHECK, HOW COPY, OVER[/bold] on the current working net.
Afterwards, the set privately reports which stations heard you and whether each received the transmission clearly or degraded. If you are inside a jammer field, the check also gives you a rough bearing toward the jammer.
## Monitor and scan
The radio can watch more than one loaded net at once.
- [bold]MONITOR[/bold] listens to every loaded net. While monitoring, [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] is disabled and the set becomes receive-only. - [bold]SCAN[/bold] also listens to every loaded net, but when one receives traffic it moves ON AIR to that memory. It stays there until another net speaks or you change it manually.
Both options are available on the guided SETTINGS tab and the expert faceplate's OPT page.
## Net log
The AN/PRC records the last [bold]50[/bold] radio lines it handled.
This includes:
- your own transmissions - traffic heard through your headset - incoming traffic on the working net - traffic from every loaded net while using MONITOR or SCAN
Enemy traffic is marked [bold]INTERCEPT[/bold].
[bold]PRINT LOG[/bold] prints the full record. [bold]PRINT INTERCEPTS[/bold] prints only intercepted traffic.
## Searching and intercepting
Operational radio frequencies are reassigned each deployment.
Capturing an enemy frequency card is one way to learn their nets. The AN/PRC's [bold]search receiver[/bold] is the other.
Search functions are controlled from the expert faceplate's SRCH page; see the expert guide for operating instructions.
[bold]While the search receiver is running, the radio leaves all loaded nets and cannot transmit.[/bold]
Intercepted messages appear in [color=#FF6B6B]red[/color] and are recorded in the net log. Only the sender's callsign is shown.
What you can actually read depends on how the transmission was sent:
- headset traffic without the correct key is heard as static - secured pack traffic without the correct key is heard as static - transmissions from an unfilled pack are readable - PT traffic is readable - CT traffic is not displayed at all
## Staking the radio down
A trained operator can turn the manpack into an unattended relay with [bold]Set Up Retrans[/bold].
Once staked down, the radio continues to relay its loaded nets without anyone wearing it. It also keeps its memories, fill card, and radio log.
Anyone standing beside a staked radio can use its handset, use its phone, or open its storage compartment.
The expert faceplate also allows a staked radio to bridge two of its loaded nets and make full use of its antenna.
There is an important downside:
[bold]Anyone can select Pack Up Radio.[/bold]
That includes the enemy. If they capture your retrans station, they take the radio, handset, and whatever fill card is still inside it.
## Fixed relays and the field mast
Manpacks are not the only source of relay coverage.
- Powered shipboard [bold]communications arrays[/bold] cover an entire ship across every deck. - Command-post [bold]antenna masts[/bold] provide 75 tiles of coverage without requiring power. - Engineers can construct a [bold]field antenna mast[/bold] almost anywhere suitable. A field mast only carries nets belonging to factions whose key has been loaded into it.
### Raising a field antenna mast
Only engineering-trained personnel can construct one.
Find [bold]antenna mast parts[/bold] in the metal-sheet construction menu, then:
1. Place the [bold]mast footing[/bold] using 40 metal. It must be on open ground, beneath open sky, outside underground areas, with enough clear space around it for guy lines and at least 20 tiles from another mast or communications array. If the location is invalid, the footing is removed and the metal is returned. 2. Wrench the footing into place, add 30 metal rods, weld the lattice, then add 15 cable for the guy lines. 3. Install a [bold]mast antenna head[/bold]. These are available from requisitions. Alternatively, construct one from an [bold]antenna head frame[/bold] using 20 metal, then add 40 plasteel, four circuit boards, and 30 cable before welding and using a multitool. 4. Plate the feed with 10 plasteel and tune it using a multitool. The feed is now open. 5. Use a [bold]COMSEC fill card[/bold] on the open feed to load that faction's key. More than one faction can be keyed into the same mast. Using a multitool on the open feed wipes every stored key. 6. Screw the feed closed and weld it. The mast is now operational.
To re-key an existing mast, including one captured from the enemy, open its feed using a screwdriver and wirecutters.
The mast carries no traffic while the feed is open.
Load the desired fill card, then close and seal the feed again.
Dismantling an open mast returns most of its construction materials along with the antenna head.
## CLF
The CLF use two combat nets:
- [bold]CLF[/bold] - the cell's normal net, available on every CLF earpiece - [bold]CLF Command[/bold] - carried only by AN/PRC radios
Both nets are relay-gated.
Unlike GOVFOR and OPFOR, the CLF have no permanent communications array. Their coverage comes from equipment they deploy themselves: the radio operator's manpack in the field and the cell's [bold]clandestine base station[/bold] at the safehouse.
- The issued CLF manpack begins already tuned to both nets, so it can be used immediately by whoever picks it up. - The clandestine base station is too heavy to wear and only operates while staked down. With a mast antenna fitted, it covers the safehouse and the surrounding approaches. - Both the Cell Leader and Radio Operator receive communications equipment and can deploy the base station or additional relay radios. - If a CLF cell loses access to both of its combat nets, it can fall back to the ungated [bold]Colony[/bold] channel. Colony is unencrypted and can be heard by anyone.
